en: I bow to the Supreme Person, the unborn Lord, the sovereign of the illustrious Yadavas, who is the singular essence of eternal bliss, pure existence and consciousness, and self-luminous. 1.
How can that which even the Veda itself observes a silence as if mute when attempting to describe it, fall within the range of the speech of us mere mortals? (2)

Even if this is known in such a way, one would still be censured [for failing to act] unless one practices the contemplation and chanting of Hari through the essential teachings of the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra). (3)
Without detachment, a person would lack the qualification for liberation, despite numerous prescribed means such as practice, knowledge, devotion, and so forth. (4)
Dispassion, self-knowledge, and devotion—these three are declared to be the primary means for liberation; among them, dispassion is said to be the state of being free from craving. || 5 ||
And that [ignorance] is concealed by "I-ness" and "mine-ness" within all bodies;
therein, "I-ness" resides in the body, while "mine-ness" resides in objects such as a wife and so forth. (6)
"What is the nature of this body, and what is its connection with sense objects?"—
when one reflects in this way, the notions of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" cease.
Through the union of a woman and a man, upon the meeting of the semen and the blood,
the individual soul (jīva), entering gradually by virtue of its own karma, assumes a body.
Within the cavity of the mother’s womb, filled with phlegm, urine,
and excrement, the living being is cooked for nine months by the flames of the digestive fire.
When, by the power of fate, at the time of birth, the infant moves crosswise, it is then extracted from here with great force, having been cut apart with surgical instruments. (10)
Or else, when it is forced out through the openings of the womb by powerful winds of birth, that suffering which then arises is likewise indescribable. (11)
What can be said of the suffering that exists even in other births, caused by mental anguish, physical disease, separation from loved ones, personal calamities, strife, and long-lasting poverty? (12)
Bound by karma, the living being wanders through the eighty-four lakh species of humans, animals, birds, and those born as lower creatures, experiencing agonizing torments. (13)
There, too, we obtained a human body; there, our birth and lineage arose; there, we engaged in the investigation of our family customs; and there, as well, the sacred scriptures were propagated.
Without the discrimination between the self and the non-self, and without the knowledge of the perishability of the body, one's own life is spent in vain even by the wise. (15)
Not even a single moment or a fraction of a second of life can be obtained anywhere for ten million pieces of gold; if all of that passes away in vain, what greater loss could there be? (16)
Since one attains the bodies of animals and so forth by transgressing the human body, what need is there to mention the ignorance regarding one's own body in this context of ultimate reality? (17)
"Alas, what misery! It is impossible for us to speak, being constantly driven by bulls, horses, donkeys, elephants, and buffaloes, exhausted and tormented by hunger. (18)
The body is a composite of blood, the three humors, marrow, fat, flesh, and bones;
it is bound on the outside by skin, and for that reason it is not eaten by crows.
Discharging phlegm and impurities from the tip of the nose and the mouth, and from the anus, one feels disgust for oneself; yet, when these have spread within, one does not perceive it.
Seeing a bone fallen on the road, he avoids it by taking another path out of fear of touching it;
yet he does not perceive his own body, which is likewise surrounded on all sides by thousands of bones. (21)
From the hair to the tips of the nails, this body is filled with a foul stench within;
yet on the outside, one smears it with agaru, sandalwood, camphor, and other perfumes.
The fool, while concealing with effort the collection of his natural defects and displaying a multitude of adventitious virtues, praises himself. (23)
If a wound that has arisen on the body is not washed for three days, many worms infested with a foul odor will emerge from it. (24)
That body which once lay asleep upon a couch adorned with a bed of beautiful flowers is now being cast into the fire, bound by ropes and wood. (25)
Seeing him seated upon the lion-throne, this world attained great joy;
yet beholding his body drawn away by Time, it closes its eyes.

This body, being of such an exceedingly impure nature, moves only by virtue of His existence; yet, forgetting that Supreme Lord, one carries a sense of "I-ness" (ego) toward this impermanent thing. (27)
Where is the self, whose nature is existence and consciousness, and where is this body composed of flesh, blood, and bone?
The wise person who feels shame at this—what does he think of another's body? (28)
The deluded man falsely attempts to wipe away the mire born of sense-objects;
yet his body, rendered sapless by the rain of misfortune, surely falls into the house [of rebirth].
A wife devoid of beauty causes agitation of the mind for men;
one who is exceedingly rich in beauty is captivated by other men. (30)
Whosoever—a stranger, a servant, or even a mendicant—beholds her, who possesses a unique and noble form, with longing desire; (31)
Upon seeing any excellent man who is exceedingly handsome compared to her own husband, does not that deer-eyed woman seek another wife for him with her very mind? (32)
Thus, the husband of the beautiful Nārī, wasting away moment by moment out of anger,
does not obtain even a trace of happiness, like a single crow among many crows at a sacrificial offering.
If a woman, being utterly ignorant, acts by transgressing her own command, she is more dangerous than even an enemy; how much more so when she covets another? (34)
Regarding the Vedic statement, "The world does not exist for one who has no son," what kind of world is being described here?
Is it liberation, or cyclic existence, or some other world? It cannot be the first. (35)
Even if all were to possess sons, the cycle of worldly existence would continue upon their liberation;
furthermore, even in the third case, the means such as hearing and so forth would become futile.
Because it serves as a means for attaining that [heaven], this Vedic teaching exists even in the second case— that of one without a son—
to prompt the performance of sacrifices such as the *putreṣṭi*.
A son is acquired through various bodily hardships and expenditures of wealth;
yet, once a son is born, the anxiety for his livelihood becomes even greater for him. (38)
Even while living, will a fool become wise, or will one who possesses good character become a paramour, a thief, a slanderer, an outcast, a lover of gambling, or a cruel man? (39)
A son who has killed his father, mother, or kinsmen is born only to cause mental anguish;
such a son contemplates the death of his father for the sake of attaining mastery over wealth and other possessions. (40)
A son endowed with all virtues may belong to someone, anywhere; yet even such a son, if he is short-lived, diseased, or childless, leads only to sorrow. (41)
If it is argued that a good rebirth comes from a son, even that is generally untenable by reason;
thus, fools seek out suffering through the hardships of the body. (42)
The union of fathers, mothers, kinsmen, sisters, paternal uncles, sons-in-law,
and others is as momentary as the meeting of travelers on a road, resulting from wandering through various births.
As long as fate is favorable and as long as there is abundant assistance from others, all are friends; conversely, when these conditions are reversed, all are enemies.
If they eat every day, they praise [the donor] like bards when they are well-satisfied; yet if it is even two or three days later, they become angry while uttering insults. (45)
The mind sets out to acquire wealth for the sake of a belly that is difficult to fill;
yet while a fortune of hundreds of thousands may remain unattained, even a mere cowrie shell is hard to find. (46)

If an additional wealth is obtained, it will become the property of one's wife and others; furthermore, there may be misfortune from kings or thieves. Therefore, the effort for wealth is in vain. || 47 ||
A king sees one who possesses wealth as unjust; a thief sees a traveler as a potential victim; a slanderer sees the onset of misfortune; and a group of kinsmen sees a quarrel.
Kings acquire wealth through numerous heaps of sins, yet that wealth is destroyed moment by moment for the sake of horses and elephants. (49)
Due to the invasion of another kingdom, defeat in battle, or the misconduct of ministers and servants;
or through poison, weapons, and secret assassination, kings are submerged in an ocean of anxiety. (50)
Sometimes he laughs, sometimes he cries; bewildered, he wanders in all directions.
At times he is joyful, at times enraged; he censures the learned and praises the wicked. (51)
For sometimes it hates something with rage, and at other times it praises itself;
the mind has become like a demon, pervaded by the rakshasi of craving.
The mind is dragged in every direction by hypocrisy, pride, greed, desire, anger, and intense envy, like a dog dragging a fallen bone along a path.
Therefore, one who is pure and dispassionate should abandon the object desired by the mind;
one should not desire that which is not so desired, and thereby one becomes free from activity.
For in this ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the unfathomable waters of sense-objects, the human body is a boat upon the water that is tossed hither and thither by the winds of karma. (55)
The living soul, like the captain of a ship, possesses nine apertures;
because these apertures are not closed, the ship is filled with water and sinks perpetually downward.
But by closing the openings [of the senses], one easily reaches the further shore;
therefore, without the restraint of the senses, no one crosses over falsehood.
A man sees another's young woman even when she is full of desire for him, and he pursues that wish;
yet, knowing well that it will not be attained, he becomes a partaker of excessive sin in vain. 58.

If one hears with one's own ears the slander of another, which is greatly delighted in by malicious people, what harm does it do to that other person? The man merely becomes a partaker of excessive sin in vain. (59)
The tongue speaks falsehood and slanders others at every moment; by this, what gain is there other than the ruin of others? Thus, a person becomes a partaker of extreme sin in vain. (60)
The pleasure that arises from the union of the sense object and the sense organ lasts for the duration of a single blink;
once the object has perished, there is suffering for as long as one lives. Thus, between these two, [the latter prevails]. (61)

Therefore, having thoroughly investigated and reached a firm certainty regarding what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted, the wise person abandons great suffering by relinquishing a small pleasure. (62)
Just as a fish, while devouring the great bait offered by a fisherman, perishes, so too does a man, while enjoying sense objects, fall when dragged down by Time (Kāla). 63.
A frog whose body is half-seized by a serpent devours hundreds of flies here;
even so, though his life-force has departed, the blind man still pursues sense-objects.
The river that carries its own rising waters reaches the ocean by way of a downward path;
if it were to remain stationary at its very source, would it not become the ocean itself? (65)
In this way, as the mind investigates its own cause, it becomes firmly established within; it no longer arises externally. Then, why would it not itself attain the state of the Self? (66)
In the rainy season, due to the accumulation of water, the water in a well becomes salty like a heavy torrent;
yet, when dried up by the summer heat, that very same water regains its sweetness.
In the same way, the mind— predominantly characterized by *tamas* and turbid due to its intensity toward sense objects—
gradually reveals *sattva* once it has been dried up by dispassion.
Even when it runs toward an object through the gateway of the external senses, longing for it, it suffers at its failure to obtain that object just as if something of its own had been lost. (69)
If the mind, wandering everywhere around mountains, cities, forts, and inaccessible rivers,
does not find its object, it becomes distressed as if constrained by a poison.
Just as a gourd placed underwater by force goes upward,
so too the mind, when fixed upon its own true nature through effort, moves outward.
Whatever fruit, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been earned here or in a previous existence by one's own karma, that very experience occurs even without being sought.
To restrain the mind-beast as it rushes headlong down the path of unwholesomeness, the Creator fashioned dispassion alone as its wooden collar. 73.
Is this pleasure experienced at the time of sleep born of the sense-objects?
Certainly not; for sleep is not the abiding of the mind in the region of the senses.
Just as a tiger confined in a house with high walls and no door remains exhausted, panting and gasping, despite its many efforts to find an exit; so it is with this [mind]. (75)
Seeing that [the mind] does not emerge due to the restraint of all the senses despite hundreds of efforts,
the consciousness remains tranquil and then attains a state of effortlessness.
Through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, through association with the virtuous, through the abandonment of latent impressions,
and through the yoga of devotion to the feet of Hari, the mind gradually relinquishes its own impetuous force.
Regarding the acquisition or the loss of another's house, wife, son, or wealth, joy and dejection are said to arise; yet how could they possibly endure for even a moment? (78)
Whether by fate some object of praise—be it small or great—is present or has passed away, one should neither rejoice nor despond upon seeing it; rather, one should dwell in the home like a guest.
A person who is devoid of the conceit of "mine" and is turned away from sense objects is not bound by actions anywhere, even while remaining in his own home. (80)
In a certain forest region, thickly covered with lush green grass and sand,
a man was lying comfortably upon the cool ground beneath the shade of a tree.
Are not the trees, rich with leaves and fruit; the fragrant, cool breezes blowing all around; and the rivers with their sweet-singing excellent birds, one's true friends? (82)
For a person who possesses the fortune of dispassion, whose mind is serene, who is free from desire,
and who enjoys the fruits that come unasked, there is fulfillment in this very life.

If, through some negligence, the substance should fall from the sprout, it would then lead to grief; but if it is offered to one who has heard the scriptures, it leads to satisfaction and spiritual welfare.
Since these sense-objects depart by their own nature, they will bring you long-lasting sorrow.
If they are abandoned of their own accord, they extend the blissful state of supreme liberation.

Having forgotten its own dwelling and wandered for a long time in the dense forest of existence, the deer of the mind—distressed by the rows of flames from the long wildfire of the three-fold suffering, leaping among worthless things with eyes wide open—is forcibly subdued by the snares of hope and slaughtered in vain by the tigers of sensory objects. (85)
Even when dispassion has arisen, happiness will not occur without awakening;
that awakening comes from the instruction of a guru, therefore one should first take refuge in a guru. 86.
Although the water belongs to the ocean, and although the wind is its impeller,
nevertheless, the cātaka bird, distressed by thirst, awaits the cloud.
It is said that there are three ways of understanding: from the scripture, from the teacher, and likewise from oneself.
Among these, understanding from the scripture comes first, just as one first hears that "molasses is sweet. (88)
Just as there is first the cognition of the guru from afar, like the sight of a sweetmeat ball;
from this [cognition] arises the cognition of the Self, like the pleasure born from eating that sweetmeat ball. || 89 ||
Taste, smell, form, sound, touch, and other objects—why are these not experienced apart from the body and the collection of sense organs? (90)

Since the collection of the dead body and senses does not know the suffering born of burning, if the vital breath were present during sleep, would it not experience the affliction caused by thieves? (91)
If the mind were the object [of its own cognition], why does it not perceive them simultaneously?
Since it is dependent on other factors, who can be the protector of one who is thus negligent? 92.
Having placed a bright lamp on the ground inside a room of dense darkness,
one should place an inverted jar with five holes upon it;
outside that, all around, one should place a flawless lute without gaps and musk.
One should place a fan made of the seven precious gems at the openings of the jars from which the sounds emerge.

Indeed, that cognition of a collection of distinct objects which arises through a portion of light—does it arise through apertures, or through a jar, or through clay, or through a vessel, or through oil, or through a thread? This is not the case; therefore, [the opponent's position] is not beautiful, as it is contradicted by direct perception (pratyakṣabādha).
Just as light is the sole refuge here for a lamp, so too does the Self abide within the body. || 94 ||
The Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness alone, indeed beheld itself as the Self;
it became that which is named "I," and from that arose the root of duality.
Therefore, it appears as a duality; thus, they become both husband and wife.
Consequently, this space is perpetually filled in a threefold manner.
"He too performed an act of seeing; from that, human beings were born"—thus the Upaniṣads declare, through the words of Yājñavalkya addressed to his beloved.
Due to the long-lasting experience of bliss, there was a certain state like deep sleep;
from that Supreme Self, however, Māyā arose as if from a dream.
This [Māyā], which is distinct from both being and non-being, is beginningless and rests upon the Reality that is the Supreme Self;
and she, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), gives birth to the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings. || 99 ||
If illusion (māyā) is indeed invisible, how could it produce a visible effect?
How can a visible cloth arise here from threads whose forms are invisible? (100)

Just as the flow of semen occurs upon the experience of sexual union in a dream, O auspicious one, while the garment remains [untouched], the sexual act is unreal; yet upon waking, the removal of the garment becomes a reality. 101.
In a dream, the man is real, the woman is unreal, and their union is false; yet the emission of semen is real. The same applies to the case under discussion. 102.
Thus, this visible world is the effect of that invisible illusion (māyā).
Indeed, this is called illusion because it bestows joy through its own destruction. 103.
Like a night that is exceedingly long, its true nature is not perceived here;
like a flash of lightning, it vanishes even as it is being scrutinized by the sages.

Māyā is said to be ignorance (avidyā) that has approached Brahman, while it is said to reside in the individual soul (jīva). It is the knot of consciousness and unconsciousness, the mind; it is to be known as imperishable until liberation. 105.

Just as the space enclosed by jars, huts, or walls is designated by those respective names, so too consciousness (caitanya) enveloped by ignorance (avidyā) is called the individual soul (jīva) in this world. 106.
Now, how could ignorance be an obscuration of Brahman, who is pure, just as darkness occurring at night cannot be an obscuration of the sun, which is self-luminous? (107)
Just as the sun is obscured by clouds produced from the rays of the sun,
the very nature of the day is not truly altered by those dense masses of distorted clouds.
Thus, although the Self is pure, it is obscured for a very long time by ignorance;
yet, the power of consciousness established in the world does not cease to exist within living beings. (109)
Within the gross body is the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), and within that is its cause;
within that too is the Great Cause, which is the Fourth (turya).
The gross [form] has been described previously; now we shall speak of the subtle and so forth.
That which the Śruti declares, "The Person is the size of a thumb," refers to the subtle [form]. (111)
The subtle elements, the vital breaths, the five sense organs, and the five [objects]—the sixteenth is the internal organ; for the aggregate of these is the subtle body (liṅgatanu). || 112 ||
That which is known as its cause is the web of latent impressions (vāsanā) within it;
the fourth state (turya), which is the support of the intellect, serves here as the cause for its manifestation.

That which is the essence of that [universe], namely the pure consciousness reflected therein, is called the *jīva* by the ancient teachers; it is that which produces the manifestation "I" within the body. (114)
Just as the reflection of the sun becomes moving due to contact with the waves of a river,
so too does there exist a flickering in consciousness because of the instability of the mind. 115.
But surely, the reflection of the sun in water and other such media illuminates a multitude of other objects; likewise, does the reflection also illuminate itself? (116)
The radiance of the sun that is reflected in vessels such as those made of bell-metal enters within the house and subsequently illuminates other objects. || 117 ||

In the same way, that reflection of consciousness which has attained the state of a living soul within the intellects illuminates external objects through the pathways of the senses, such as the eyes. (118)
Therefore, whoever among the noble ones knows thus—"I am Brahman"—he indeed becomes this All; for even the gods are not masters over his prosperity.
He who thinks "I am one and that [deity] is another," and thus knows while worshipping another deity, possesses a self belonging to those [beings], and he is like a beast. (120)
Thus, the Upaniṣads, the Śruti, and the words of the Blessed Lord declare this;
and here, too, there is the reasoning that "the man of knowledge is indeed the Self"—this is my conviction.
Whether straight or crooked, wood consumed by fire attains the state of fire; so what need is there for it to be grasped by the hand, even though it possesses a straight or crooked form? (122)
Thus, the person who is established in the self and whose form is that of the self arises;
though he appears as if embodied, in reality he is the absolute, solitary Self.
Just as the single sun is reflected in many vessels of water, so too is that Supreme Self, though one, present within many bodies. 124.
If, by chance, a single vessel is broken, does the sun dissolve?
And because of the flickering of its reflection, does the sun itself become flickering? || 125 ||
Just as the single sun performs its own function by means of its light,
so too does this world of moving and non-moving beings move by virtue of the existence of the one Self.
By the same water by which the plantain, the campaka, the jasmine, and other plants flourish, those very same roots, onions, and garlic possess distinct tastes and fragrances. (127)
For a single carpenter here, by means of his profound skill, simultaneously causes many wooden forms to dance upon the top beam of a pillar. || 128 ||

Just as molasses, sugar-candy, granulated sugar, and so forth, are distinct transformations of a single sugarcane, and just as armlets, bracelets, and the like are various differentiations of a single piece of gold; || 129 ||
Thus, the world—varied in its nature, varied in its form, and varied in its activity—moves on loftily by means of that single Self alone. (130)

As long as the traveler on the path does not eat the food prepared and held for him by the aggregates, so long will he not experience the afflictions of contact, fear, or hunger once that food has been consumed. (131)
He who perceives the Lord of the World as the thread running through humans, elephants, buffaloes, dogs, pigs, and so forth—he alone enjoys non-dual bliss. 132.
Just as when the sun has risen, people carry out their own activities, yet the sun neither performs them nor causes them to be performed, so it is with the Self as well. 133.
When iron is pervaded by fire and struck by other pieces of iron, could there be any suffering born of that impact for the fire contained within it? || 134 ||
Even when wood is being cut by the blows of a harsh axe, can the fire dwelling within it be cut by those blows? It is just like that.
The Śruti also declares repeatedly: "Another, not eating, looks on," and so forth.
When a lamp shines in a house at night, a thief steals the wealth;
does the lamp likewise urge him on or restrain him? So too is it with the self. (137)
When some event occurs or perishes by the power of fate at the edge of a house, does the lamp feel joy or distress? Tell me, is the self likewise? (138)
Although the sun, the moon, fire, lamps, and so forth may be illuminators of both themselves and others, nevertheless, by none of these is the Self ever illuminated. (139)
The manifestation of these [objects] must occur through the eye-door by means of another self;
otherwise, those objects would not be known from mere light alone. (140)
Even in that case, if the self does not act as an assistant through the gateway of the eyes, then how could a blind person see objects when there is light? (141)

Even if the self were real, why would there be no cognition of it? If that [cognition] were to occur through another sense organ, then indeed, when the connection with the eyes is obstructed in a blind person, an object appears through contact with the hand. (142)
"He knows by what all [is known], and by what could that [knower] itself be known?"—such is the teaching of the Upaniṣads; therefore, the Self is bound by the self. 143.
For as long as one contemplates one's own true nature for even a moment or half a moment, so long will the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) be heard in the right ear. 144.
Indeed, the supreme investigation of the *nāda* is the indicator of the mind’s success, its commencement, its steadiness, its rest, its confidence, and the purity of its seed. (145)
The mind finds delight for a moment in the sound of beaten drums, clay drums, conchs, and the like;
how much more so, then, in this unstruck (anāhata) sound, which is honey-sweet, undivided, and pure? 146.
Just as the mind attains stillness through the cessation of sense objects, so too is the sound heard, becoming increasingly prolonged like that of a flute. 147.
If the mind is absorbed for a long time in that light which dwells within the nāda, it will not lead to bondage in saṃsāra again. (148)

Due to the experience of supreme bliss and the long-term contemplation of the internal sound (nāda), this dissolution of the mind is the most excellent, even among the many other forms of dissolution. 149.
Having attained supreme bliss, the mind never at any time or place wavers, though it was once scorched by the heat of saṃsāra and exhausted by wandering through various wombs. 150.
When the mind reaches a state of stillness, wondering, "What is this? Who am I? To whom do I belong? due to being filled with the bliss of non-duality, then it becomes as if swooned. 151.
Through long-term self-experience, the mind arises in the form of the Self; like a river that has flowed into the ocean, it attains the state of the ocean itself. 152.
The mind that has entered into the Self no longer looks toward sense objects;
just as clarified butter extracted from milk does not return to the state of milk in this world. (153)
When the mind is dissolved— that is, when it has reached its end— into that mere manifestation which is woven through the vision, the seer, and the seen, then it becomes swooned (mūrchita). || 154 ||
When [the object] comes face-to-face with itself, or when it is merely seen, then [this occurs];
for indeed, the distinction between the seen and the seer does not exist when this [object] is not face-to-face. || 155 ||
Indeed, within the single pure consciousness, the seer and the rest arise in a threefold manner;
when that triad has dissolved, only the pure consciousness remains thereafter.
Just as the face exists both before and after the mirror, yet its reflection appears within it;
and even when the mirror is destroyed, the face remains, so too does the Self exist within the face [of the world]. 157.
Whatever sweetness exists in a lump of jaggery, it exists even in a minute fraction of it;
likewise, there is no separate existence between the jaggery and its sweetness. (158)
Or rather, just as there is no difference between the camphor and its fragrance, so too the world attains the nature of the self for men whose minds have become one with the nature of the Self. 159.
If there should be an experience of existence at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking, and if that [experience] were stable within, then one indeed attains non-dual bliss. (160)
In the vast, exceedingly deep, and shoreless ocean of consciousness, knowledge, and bliss, the series of waves that are living beings flickers, tossed by the winds of karma. 161.
When the fierce-rayed sun of consciousness has risen and blazed forth, the manifold mirages of living beings flicker everywhere as mere falsehoods. 162.
When that [Reality] is seen within, this entire world appears shimmering from afar;
yet when that is seen even once, it dissolves somewhere into a state of non-existence. (163)
Filled both within and without, he is submerged in the ocean of supreme bliss, like a jar that has long been immersed in the great lake of the daughter of Jahnu. 164.
In Hari—the fullness of fullness, higher than the highest, whose further shore is unknown;
who is an ocean of the nectar of the expansion of consciousness, devoid of waves, ripples, and the like;
and who is the supreme light that illuminates the quarters and the sky with the brilliance of ten million suns—[I take refuge].
For those whose minds are immersed in the singular essence of their own bliss, there is neither you, nor I, nor the world.
When a being arises in the mind, the dawning of awakening occurs like a flash of lightning;
at that very moment, it would become stable if the mind attains purity. (166)
Indeed, the inner self is not purified except through devotion to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa;
the mind is cleansed by devotion, just as a garment is washed with alkaline solutions. 167.
Just as a face is clearly reflected for a long time in a mirror that has been thoroughly purified by ashes and other means, so too does knowledge manifest in a pure mind. (168)
Let those who are wise through devotion to Hari know the seed therein:
the two forms of Brahman are indeed both the manifest and the unmanifest. (169)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad; or rather, these two paths taught by the Blessed One lead to liberation—either through hardship or without hardship—between these two.
Devotion to Hari is declared to be twofold: gross and subtle.
At the beginning, it is gross; and from that, the subtle arises.

The constant performance of the duties of one's own stage of life, the perpetual festival of worshipping the image of Kṛṣṇa, and eternal association with the servants of Hari through the performance of various services. 172.
There is a great festival in listening to the stories of Kṛṣṇa and a commitment to truthful speech;
there is an aversion toward another’s young wife, toward wealth, and toward slandering others. (173)

Distaste for vulgar talk, devotion to journeys to sacred pilgrimage sites, and the reflection that one’s life has been spent in vain during separation from the Lord of the Yadus—[these are the signs of a devotee]. 174.
When one performs devotion in this way, a subtle form of devotion arises, born from the grace of the narrations of Kṛṣṇa, through which Hari enters within.
The practice of mental worship toward the form of Hari as heard through the words of the Smṛtis and the Purāṇas has the purpose of [attaining Him] even while residing among one's kinsmen. (176)
Truth consists in the knowledge that Kṛṣṇa resides within all living beings;
from that arises non-malice toward the multitude of creatures, and from that, compassion for all beings. (177)
Contentment with whatever is obtained by chance, freedom from the sense of "mine" regarding wife, children, and so forth, and consequently, the absence of egoism and anger. (178)

Gentle speech, serenity, equanimity toward self-reproach and praise, endurance of the dualities of pleasure and pain or cold and heat, and fearlessness in the face of calamity—[these are the marks of a noble person]. 179.
Indifference toward sleep, food, and recreation; freedom from attachment;
no room for idle speech; and eternal peace through the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa. || 180 ||
When the song of Hari is sung by someone, or when the sound of the flute is heard, the manifestation of bliss occurs simultaneously with the emergence of the joyful *sāttvika* emotions. (181)
While that bliss of the Supreme Self is being experienced by the mind held in firm grasp,
once that [bliss] has attained stability, the mind reaches a state like that of an elephant intoxicated with rut.

When one gradually perceives the state of the Lord within all beings and all beings within the Lord, if such a condition arises, then at that very moment one becomes a supreme devotee of Hari. || 183 ||
In the most delightful forest of Vṛndāvana situated near the banks of the Yamunā, upon the ground beneath a wish-fulfilling tree, he placed one foot atop the other. || 184 ||
Standing here, dark blue as a rain cloud, illuminating the entire universe with his own splendor,
clad in yellow garments, and with all his limbs anointed with sandalwood and camphor.
With eyes reaching to his ears, his ears adorned with a pair of earrings, his lotus-face graced by a gentle smile, and wearing the noble Kaustubha gem along with a string of pearls; 185.
He was not adorning his own ornaments such as bracelets and rings;
with a forest garland dangling from his neck, he had dispelled the Kali age by his own splendor.
Meditate upon Hari dwelling within a grove, eating together with the cowherds, his head adorned with clusters of *guñjā* berries and resonant with their jingling sounds. 188.

Bow down to the Great Being, the bestower of supreme bliss, whose feet are joined by the Mandākinī river, who is served by gentle breezes scented with mandāra flowers, and who is the embodiment of ultimate joy. 189.

Bow down to the Yādava, who has perfumed the circle of the quarters with hundreds of fragrances, who is always surrounded on all sides by sweet-smelling scents, and who is most intensely fragrant through the destruction of the afflictions of worldly existence. 190.

Having abandoned Kṛṣṇa— who is more beautiful than ten million gods of love, who bestows desired fruits, and who is an ocean of compassion— what other object would my pair of eyes venture to behold? (191)
Having abandoned the most meritorious, exceedingly sweet, and heart-delighting narration of Hari, how can one's pair of ears show such devotion to vulgar [talk]? 192.

Indeed, it is the misfortune of the senses that they become attached to other objects—even though those objects are momentary, productive of evil, and subject to decay—while Kṛṣṇa is their eternal object. 193.
That unity between the qualified and the quality-transcendent which has been proclaimed in the Vedas and the Mahāpurāṇas in a cryptic manner, I shall now declare with extremely clear meaning. (194)

The inner controller within all beings, consisting of knowledge, being, consciousness, and bliss, beyond primordial nature, the Supreme Self—he who is the ornament of the Yadu clan is indeed this very one. 195.
But surely he possesses qualities, has a visible body, and dwells in a specific location;
how then could he be the Supreme Self, endowed with passion and anger like an ordinary being? (196)
All other visible objects are perceived by this eye;
however, the Blessed One, who is accessible only through the vision of knowledge, is not perceived by this sight. (197)
Since the Blessed One bestowed divine vision upon Pārtha at the time of the manifestation of the universal form,
it is therefore appropriate that Nṛhari remains invisible.
Just as the orb of the sun, though situated in one place, is perceived directly as being round, so too does it illuminate the universe; it is seen by all everywhere simultaneously. (199)
Although this Lord of the Yadus appears as one possessing form and as a localized portion,
he is nevertheless omnipresent, the self of all, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The Blessed One enjoyed himself simultaneously with many gopīs;
or rather, Hari [enjoyed himself] simultaneously with Videha Janaka and Śrutadeva Bhūdeva.
Then Duryodhana beheld his own army appearing black;
therefore, the all-pervading Self, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign Kṛṣṇa [is so named]. || 202 ||
When the Śrīvatsa struck the chest of the Lord of Śrī, was it an object of hatred?
Is the fruit the same for devotees, asuras, or others? (203)
Therefore, there is no one who is our enemy, nor our friend, nor even neutral;
for the Lord of the Yadus, Nṛhari, established upon the path of the righteous, is fruitful like a tree.
Just as iron attains the state of gold when it is struck by a mass of iron rods upon a touchstone, so too does one attain [the state of a friend] even through the enmity of enemies. || 205 ||
Surely this continuum of living beings has arisen from the Self; yet, since the Self is dearer than the world, it is impossible for [the world] to be of that same nature. (206)

At the time of the calves' abduction, Hari created from himself gopas together with their calves, each possessing distinct ages, forms, dispositions, and ornaments, in order to create a delusion for Aja (Brahmā).
"Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire"—in order to demonstrate the meaning of this Vedic scripture, He created the multitude of individual souls from His own body. (208)
Once, while Kṛṣṇa and the noble cowherds were herding the calves in the groves on the banks of the Yamunā, she herself wandered nearby among the excellent cattle-pens.
Beholding their calf from afar, the cows, agitated by affection, rushed toward it;
and being difficult to restrain, they proceeded even against the cowherds.
With their udders flowing profusely from the weight of their milk, the cows— possessing young calves— licked them with their broad tongues as before and joyfully caused them to drink.
The cowherds also took their own children upon their heads and smelled them; thus, for that moment, their acquisition of the supernatural grew there. 212.
Previously, the cowherds and the calves were indeed of the nature of Kṛṣṇa;
by that, Kṛṣṇa demonstrated his own dearness toward them.
"The Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, and dearer than everything else; for it is the innermost"—thus has the truth been declared by the Upaniṣads. (214)
Surely the Self, Hari, dwells equally within all beings, whether high or low; how then has He come to possess a state of superiority or inferiority in Duryodhana or Arjuna? (215)
Deaf, blind, lame, and mute; tall, short, and handsome—all were seen by him through his power, along with their calves, cowherds, and four arms. || 216 ||
The equality of all beings with Nṛhari—whether it be with a mosquito or a serpent, or with the three worlds—is directly proclaimed by the Upaniṣads. 217.
If Vāsudeva is indeed the Self, which is by its very nature a non-enjoyer, how can he take delight with the wives of others through various deceitful efforts? (218)
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, who possessed a beautiful and ever-new form, the gopīs were utterly infatuated;
longing for him in their minds out of desire, they experienced the agony of separation. || 219 ||
Whether walking, standing, intent on household chores, or eating,
they never perceived any object other than Kṛṣṇa, even when it was right before their eyes.
In the delusion born of their unbearable separation, they saw trees, men, and even animals as their own husbands;
thinking, "This is Hari," they embraced them with great joy and impetuosity.
And Vyāsa Nārāyaṇa himself has declared that a certain girl, acting as Kṛṣṇa, drank from the breast of another girl who was acting as Pūtanā. 222.

Therefore, upon seeing their own respective beloveds in the form of Kṛṣṇa, Hari— the inner controller— manifested visibly before the wives of the kings of Vraja, who were themselves the consorts of other monarchs.
When analyzed from the perspective of ultimate reality, according to the analogy of the sweetness of molasses, even this transient human body attains the form of the Supreme Self. 224.
How much more so, then, the extraordinary deeds of the Lord Nṛhari, who possesses infinite power and assumes a body for his divine play, performing these acts here through his own *māyā*.
When his mother was enraged by his eating clay and had her face opened wide, he showed her the entire universe within it; how much more so, then, could he who is the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa)?
Pūtanā came to the house to make him drink from her pair of breasts, which were as dangerous as poison;
for that woman of vast fortune, her very body was destined for surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa brought the demon Śakaṭa, though he had committed an offense, close to him; out of the special affection of an embrace around the neck, he forgave the demon from his childhood.
Having uprooted the twin *yama* and *arjuna* trees, Nṛhari, who had been long distressed while confined within the mortar,
now reaches his own abode, moving about upon the courtyard ground.
By him, the eternal enemy of the gods was [defeated], and Keśin was brought under the power of death;
even a certain wretched crow and a crane went to the world free from sorrow.
The Blessed One turned the sinless Aghāsura— who was violently crushing the multitude of cows, cowherd girls, and cowherds— into a vast serpent-king.
Having drunk the forest fire,
the ocean of compassion protected all the bewildered cowherds who had been scorched by its unbearable heat.
May Kṛṣṇa protect Gokula, which was distressed by showers of thunderbolts and lightning;
he alone, with one hand, held up Mount Govardhana aloft.
Having struck with the surface of a stone a washerman who was running away out of greed for his clothes,
He forgot that offense and granted him residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
By means of garlands and sandalwood paste, he made the hunchbacked woman— whose body was crooked, whose lips were very long, and whose speech faltered due to her physical deformity— straight-faced.
Slain by Hari with the tip of his hoof, Kuvalayāpīḍa fell like a tall,
intoxicated elephant before a lamp falling upon a moth.
Under the pretext of a wrestling match, having attained physical contact with Śrī Raṅga on the arena,
those known as Muṣṭika and Cāṇūra immediately attained the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
Because of an offense committed by his own body, Kaṃsa— the ornament of the Yadu lineage— was destroyed by Him whose inner self yearned for Vaikuṇṭha.
To him who was immersing himself in the Pṛthuraṇa-tīrtha through the yoga of beholding Hari,
the Blessed One indeed granted immediate union (sāyujya) with Himself, even as he was [still] a Caidya.
Through incarnations such as the Fish and others, many enemies of the gods have been slain;
they were restored to their own true forms—so what need is there to speak of liberation? (240)
Those who were slain by the joy of the Yadus did not undergo rebirth again;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa is the inner controller and the impeller of all incarnations. (241)
He who showed Brahmā many cosmic eggs, and within each egg, the most wonderful cowherds with their calves, as well as all the Viṣṇus and the Unborn One (Aja);
and Śambhu, who bears upon his own head the water from whose feet flows from the three forms.
Kṛṣṇa indeed exists as something distinct, unchanging, consisting of pure being and consciousness, and characterized by the quality of dark-blue.
He for whom Śiva, the enemy of Tripura, is an object of compassion; he whose pure daughter, the dweller in the lotus (Lakṣmī), is the water used for washing the nails of his feet;
and he who, though all-powerful, considers even the sovereignty over the three worlds a mere gift.
May he, our family deity, the Lord of the Yadus, who is the source of our lineage, be victorious!
O Mother, having placed me— who am born from the root of delusion— into the hands of Māyā for the sake of being maintained, you have long remained indifferent toward me under the name of Kṛṣṇa.
O sole abode of compassion, you do not look upon my face even once.
O Omniscient One, you are not able to bring about the pacification of the root; why indeed is this so? (244)
O dear one, you are indifferent, steadfast, eternally devoid of qualities, and free from attachment; what could be more wretched than this state of existence here?
If you do not suddenly bestow your affection upon us, then that— [The text provided appears to be incomplete.]
Dwell once again within this pure interior of your own belly.
O Lord of the world, why do you, the Sovereign, cause suffering to those who have taken refuge in you?

Why does the lotus contract when the orb of the fierce-rayed sun has risen? If it is certain that the enjoyment on earth of men comes from their previously accumulated karma, [then why this distress?]
Indeed, that [strength] of yours has been overcome by those powerful Dānava kings who are nourished by men. || 246 ||

Having emerged from the ocean of the nectar of eternal bliss, this dark cloud—drawn forth by the heavy gales of longing in the hearts of the virtuous—now rains down the wondrous nectar of realized wisdom through the streams of its own words.
O Cātaka bird of the mind, if you do not desire this, then you are either possessed by falsehood or you are asleep. What else? (247)
Abandoning the fickleness of the mind, fix its two tips before you; place all sense-objects at one end and the Lord of Śrī at the other.
Alas, consider now which of these two provides true rest and ultimate benefit!
Or, wherever there is supreme bliss through reasoning or through direct experience, that should be cultivated. || 248 ||
One is not so eager for sons, grandsons, wives, other young women, wealth, or other riches— even for food and such things— according to their relative degree of excellence,
as one is when the infinite and all-pervading Lord, the leader of the Yadus, has arisen in the heart.
For he wanders at will and without fear in the ocean of the nectar of intense bliss. || 249 ||
Others daily strive for some desired fruit through the worship of deities for specific boons, or for heaven and liberation through other means such as yoga and sacrifice;
but for us, who seek only the focused meditation upon the pair of feet of the Joy of the Yadus—
What is the use of the world, what is the use of self-restraint, what is the use of a king, and what is the use of heaven and liberation?
The Lord of Śrī draws toward Himself even a person who has merely sought refuge,
just as a magnet attracts even iron.
It is merely like an insentient object present before one's eyes. || 251 ||
"This one is superior, this one is inferior"—
whether by birth, appearance, wealth, or age; whether praiseworthy or blameworthy— it is thus [that people judge].
The Blessed One does not perceive [this] at the time of bestowing grace.
Therefore, the inner self, which experiences the internal states, is like a great cloud,
or like a khadira or campaka tree.
What does the raining down investigate? || 253||
Although Nṛhari is equal toward all everywhere, nevertheless,
these devotees delight in supreme bliss through his compassionate glance.
Just as the young turtles, having no other refuge and lacking food such as milk, survive solely by the gaze of affection, so too do those who have no other resort. (255)
Although the sky is empty, nevertheless, by means of the cloud and the moon,
it fulfills the hope of those named the cātaka and the cakora bird due to their firm devotion.
In the same way, although Hari is beyond the reach of the sight, speech, and mind of men,
he nonetheless bears fruit by his grace all of a sudden with an abundant nectar of true bliss.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
The Prabodhasudhākara is completed.
